subject: Cooking
title: Conduction: Heat Through Direct Contact
description: A 60-second lesson on Conduction: Heat Through Direct Contact.

hook.text: A steak sizzles the instant it touches a hot pan. That sound is conduction at work.

buildup.text: Conduction transfers heat through direct contact between molecules vibrating into their neighbors.

discovery.text: Copper conducts 25 times better than stainless steel — that's why chefs prize copper pans.

twist.text: But copper reacts with acidic foods, so it must be lined with tin or steel to stay safe.

climax.text: The best pan isn't the hottest — it's the one that spreads heat most evenly across its surface.

punchline.text: Great searing starts with understanding contact.

quiz.question: Which metal conducts heat about 25 times better than stainless steel?

details.summary: Conduction transfers heat through direct physical contact between molecules. A hot pan heats food touching its surface, and heat slowly conducts inward. Metal conducts heat faster than food, which is why pan material and thickness dramatically affect cooking results.
details.whyItMatters: Conduction is the primary heat transfer in sauteing, grilling, and pan-frying. Choosing the right cookware material depends on understanding how efficiently it conducts heat.
takeaways: Heat transfers molecule to molecule through direct contact
Copper conducts heat five times faster than stainless steel
Thick pans distribute heat more evenly than thin ones

faq.question: Why do copper pans heat more evenly?
faq.answer: Copper's thermal conductivity is roughly five times that of stainless steel. Heat spreads across the entire surface quickly, eliminating hot spots. This precision makes copper ideal for delicate sauces that scorch easily on uneven surfaces.

faq.question: Why does cast iron retain heat so well?
faq.answer: Cast iron has high thermal mass due to its density and thickness. It absorbs and stores a large amount of energy, so it maintains temperature when cold food is added. However, it heats unevenly because iron conducts poorly compared to aluminum or copper.
